performers: Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra; Fritz Reiner, conductor
intro: Bartók sends his wind players out two by two, each pair keeping its own distance between notes. A brass chorale interrupts their parade; when the bassoons return, a third player tags along.

sections.label: Intro · Side drum alone
sections.mNote: Seven bars on the drum, with the snares off

sections.label: A · Five wind duets
sections.mNote: Bassoons, oboes, clarinets, flutes, then muted trumpets

sections.label: B · Brass chorale over the drum
sections.mNote: Long brass chords; the drum keeps its little pattern

sections.label: A′ · Two bassoons become three
sections.mNote: The duets return with extra players winding around them

sections.label: Coda · Winds hold, drum finishes
sections.mNote: The wind chord fades; the side drum has the last word

cues.title: A drum without snares
cues.text: The side drum begins alone, with its snares switched off. Seven bars of dry taps introduce the first pair: two bassoons, moving together a sixth apart over plucked strings.
cues.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, plate B. & H. 9009, p. 29, bars 1–24. The drum is marked “without snares”; the bassoons begin in bar 8: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Oboes closer together
cues.text: The oboes keep only a third between them. Their tune has its own quick turns and little pauses; the bassoons’ wide-stepping duet has left the stage.
cues.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, p. 30, bars 25–44: oboe duet in thirds over strings. The interval scheme is also described by Brett Van Gansbeke: https://www.orchestralbassoon.com/bartok-concerto
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The scherzo gets an exemption
cues.text: For the Boston première in 1944, Bartók describes the concerto’s progress from sternness to a “life-assertion” in the finale. He makes one cheerful exception: this “jesting second movement”.
cues.evidence: Bartók’s programme note for the Boston première, 1 December 1944, reproduced by Brett Van Gansbeke, citing Béla Bartók Essays, edited by Benjamin Suchoff, p. 431: https://www.orchestralbassoon.com/bartok-concerto

cues.title: Same beat, brass choir
cues.text: The trumpets take off their mutes for a five-part brass chorale. The notes stretch out, yet Bartók marks the same tempo. Beneath the solemn chords, the drum carries on with its little pattern.
cues.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, pp. 36–37, from bar 123: lo stesso tempo, trumpets senza sordino, trombones, tuba and side drum; horns join later: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A third bassoon joins
cues.text: The original bassoon pair returns, still a sixth apart. A third bassoon wriggles beneath them in quicker notes. The plucked string accompaniment is back too.
cues.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, pp. 37–38, bars 164–180: the returning duet gains a third bassoon marked staccato: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The drum closes the door
cues.text: The strings stop and the winds hold a last chord. The side drum, still without snares, finishes the movement on its own: the same dry taps that let everybody in.
cues.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, p. 46, bars 252–263: the strings withdraw, the wind chord fades and the side drum completes the close: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The bassoons step out
transitions.how: After seven bars of side drum, the two bassoons begin their duet in sixths. Second violins, violas, cellos and double basses pluck a spare accompaniment. The drum dwindles to isolated taps and falls silent; the bassoons keep the same Allegretto scherzando pace.
transitions.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, p. 29, bars 1–24: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf

transitions.title: The trumpets take off their mutes
transitions.to: B · Brass chorale over the drum
transitions.how: The trumpet duet and strings settle on held notes while the drum resumes its opening rhythm. At lo stesso tempo, two unmuted trumpets and two trombones begin the chorale, with tuba below. The beat stays unchanged beneath the longer notes.
transitions.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, p. 36, bars 120–129: the chorale begins at bar 123: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf

transitions.title: Two bassoons acquire a companion
transitions.from: B · Brass chorale over the drum
transitions.how: Short flute, oboe and clarinet figures stir above the last held horn and tuba chord. The bassoons reclaim their opening tune over plucked strings. This time a third bassoon runs beneath the duet, marked staccato.
transitions.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, pp. 37–38, bars 158–180: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf

transitions.title: The wind chord outlasts the strings
transitions.how: The strings stop after their last held chord. Flutes, oboes, clarinets and bassoons repeat a chord, then sustain it over the horns. The side drum returns underneath, without snares. As the winds fall silent, its taps dwindle to pianissimo.
transitions.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, p. 46, bars 248–263: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf

source.title: Bartók, Concerto for Orchestra, B. & H. 9009, II
source.locator: Boosey & Hawkes full score, printed pp. 29–46: five wind duets, brass chorale, returning duets and the side-drum close.

timeline.note: The side drum begins alone, with its snares off (p. 29).
Two bassoons move in sixths over plucked strings (p. 29).
Oboes play in thirds; the strings alternate plucked and bowed notes, with a brief drum reply (p. 30).
The two clarinets play their duet in sevenths over strings (pp. 30–32).
Flutes in fifths take over, with a quiet timpani stroke and strings beneath them (pp. 32–34).
Muted trumpets play in seconds over divided strings (pp. 34–35).
The brass chorale stretches long notes above the side drum’s short pattern (pp. 36–37).
A third bassoon winds beneath the returning duet; strings pluck the accompaniment (pp. 37–38).
Clarinets join the returning oboes, with a timpani stroke and string replies below (p. 39).
The strings stop; winds and horns hold a chord above the returning side drum (p. 46).
The side drum finishes alone, dwindling to pianissimo (p. 46).

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: The Archive explicitly identifies Pittsburgh, 1946. Its stored AcoustID resolves to a Pittsburgh/Reiner recording, corroborating that attribution rather than merely comparing durations. This is not the Chicago Symphony/RCA recording of 22 October 1955. The fingerprint database is supplementary, community-maintained evidence, not a fresh comparison performed here.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Orchestral version; Reiner’s corrected conducting score, with Bartók’s revised finale ending.
fields.note: Móricz identifies the performing source as Reiner’s tissue proof CR, corrected by Bartók, and explicitly associates the 1946 recording with the new ending. The 1946 printed score is consulted for broad orchestration, not represented as Reiner’s exact performing copy; minor textual differences are not timed here. The Archive description mistakenly gives BB 127, which belongs to Piano Concerto No. 3.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The critical edition identifies this range for the complete recording. The Sony discographical transcription gives 5 February for CD 5 tracks 1–5; individual movement/session allocation is not established. Neither the 1948 issue nor 2010 upload is a session date.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: Venue stated in the reproduced Columbia session discography. No microphone position or engineer is established for the selected transfer.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: This identifies the original commercial recording, not the unidentified physical or digital carrier from which the Archive MP3 was copied.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The discographical transcription dates MM-793 to 22 November 1948 and ML 4102 to 7 February 1949. Douglas Watt’s March 1949 review independently identifies Columbia set 793 and ML-4102 as the same Pittsburgh/Reiner performance. The exact carrier used by public-domain-archive.com remains unknown; no sleeve or label scans accompany the selected Archive item.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: Complete set: XCO 35800–35811, take 1; LP matrices xLP 539 (I–II), xLP 540 (III–V)
fields.note: These are complete-recording identifiers transcribed from Sony’s discography, not an asserted side-by-side mapping for this MP3. Individual movement matrix boundaries, transfer-side joins and the transferred pressing are unknown. DAHR’s opened Reiner listing does not include these Columbia masters; no DAHR matrix record is fabricated.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: Archive says only that the files were taken from public-domain-archive.com. Neither transfer engineer nor restoration producer is named. The uploader is not treated as the transfer engineer.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The Archive public date, 8 August 2010, and file modification dates describe repository activity, not the date of analogue transfer or mastering.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: Original digitisation, equalisation, noise reduction, editing, speed correction and the source carrier are unestablished. The item calls the selected file an original VBR MP3 and supplies Ogg derivatives; this does not identify how the historical master was transferred.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Public domain in the EU under the ordinary life-plus-70 term; not a worldwide clearance.
fields.note: Bartók died in 1945; IMSLP identifies this score as public domain in life-plus-70 countries and explicitly warns of continuing US protection. The critical-edition commentary is cited as scholarship, not redistributed as a public-domain score.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — territorial EU public domain: first lawful publication in 1948, before 1963.
fields.note: Móricz’s source RecR states first released in 1948; the Columbia discography identifies MM-793 and its 22 November 1948 issue. A contemporary March 1949 review independently establishes that the recording was commercially available as Columbia set 793 and ML-4102. This is a publication basis anywhere, not an assumption from the 1946 session. Its former 50-year term had expired before the 2013 extension. US sound-recording status is not established. The Archive’s legacy public-domain URL alone is not relied upon; it is an uploader declaration, not proof of the performers’ release.

composer.born: 25 March 1881, Nagyszentmiklós, Hungary (now Sânnicolau Mare, Romania)
composer.epithet: He heard a future for concert music in village songs, and went out with a phonograph to learn how they were sung.
facts: István Thomán, a Liszt pupil, and Hans Koessler; Budapest Academy, 1899–1903
Piano professor in Budapest, 1907–34; folk-music research in Budapest and at Columbia University
Hungarian, Slovak and Romanian villages; Biskra, 1913; Turkey with Adnan Saygun, 1936
Six quartets, three piano concertos, two violin concertos, three stage works and Mikrokosmos
composer.background:
In 1904 Bartók heard Lidi Dósa, a young woman from Transylvania, singing to the children in her care. He wrote down her songs. Here was Hungarian music unlike the urban entertainment that usually went by that name, and he wanted more of it. Two years later, collecting with Bartók, the writer Béla Balázs found that the frail-looking pianist could wear him out: “I was already very tired, but he kept urging and driving me on to collect more!” Balázs put the encounter in his diary.

Bartók was born in Nagyszentmiklós in 1881, when the town belonged to Hungary; it is now Sânnicolau Mare in Romania. His father, director of an agricultural school, died when he was seven. His mother Paula supported Béla and his sister by teaching, moving between towns before settling in Pozsony, now Bratislava. At the Budapest Academy he studied piano with István Thomán, who had studied with Liszt, and composition with Hans Koessler.
